## Equivalence

Overall: **PASSED** (full workload).

| workload | N_max legacy / new | descriptors: max abs diff (violations) | energies, same weights: max abs / rel diff | passed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2000× aspirin-like | [20, 11] / [20, 11] | local_matrix 0.0e+00 (0), local_numbers 0.0e+00 (0), long_range_matrix 0.0e+00 (0), long_range_features 0.0e+00 (0) | 2.67e-05 / 1.0e-06 (\|E\| ≤ 42, 0 violations) | yes |
| 200× stachyose-like | [85, 58] / [85, 58] | local_matrix 0.0e+00 (0), local_numbers 0.0e+00 (0), long_range_matrix 0.0e+00 (0), long_range_features 0.0e+00 (0) | 7.63e-05 / 6.4e-07 (\|E\| ≤ 136, 0 violations) | yes |

* Descriptors: atol = rtol = 1e-06, integer columns exact, after reordering the legacy rows (cell traversal order) into input order. Model: `legacy-head` architecture, `assignment = "legacy"`.
* Energies: legacy model built with seed, weights exported in construction order and loaded with `lrmlp.model.assign_legacy_weights`; rtol 1e-05, atol 1e-05 per atom. New energies come from `Potential.predict` (positions → descriptors → batched model).
* XLA: 100 training steps with `jit_compile=false` and `true` from the same weights and data order: max rel. weight diff 4.3e-05 (|w| > 1e-3), max abs 4.0e-06, rel. diff of the mean loss 1.5e-07 (largest per-step rel. loss diff 2.7e-04, reported only) → passed (rtol 0.0001).
* `steps_per_execution` 8 vs 1, one epoch (1600 steps): max abs weight diff 0.0e+00, rel. loss diff 0.0e+00 → passed.

## `steps_per_execution` and `jit_compile`

| steps_per_execution | jit_compile=false | jit_compile=true | XLA gain |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 314 | 556 | +77 % |
| 8 | 378 | 720 | +91 % |

Gain of `steps_per_execution = 8` over 1: +20 % without XLA, +30 % with XLA.

Rule: a default changes only with a gain of at least 15 % and a passed equivalence check. The benchmark itself never changes defaults. Settings of the measured code: TrainConfig default `steps_per_execution = 8`, `jit_compile = false`; thesis presets `steps_per_execution = 8`, `jit_compile = true`.

* `train.jit_compile`: gain +77 % / +91 % (K = 1 / 8), equivalence passed → **recommend `jit_compile = true`** (where it is set: see the settings above).
* `train.steps_per_execution`: gain +20 %, equivalence passed → **recommend `steps_per_execution = 8`**.

XLA compiles the step once per input shape. The atom axis is `None` in the signature, so a dataset with molecules of different sizes would compile once per size; every dataset of the thesis holds a single molecule (one shape), the benchmark as well.

## Missed targets

* Preprocessing, mol/s, 1 process (2000× aspirin-like (G-A)): 16.83× instead of ≥ 20×.
* Bytes per molecule on disk (factor = smaller) (2000× aspirin-like (G-A)): 0.45× instead of ≥ 3×.
* Bytes per molecule on disk (factor = smaller) (200× stachyose-like (G-C)): 0.47× instead of ≥ 3×.
* Input pipeline, mol/s (1 epoch, no model) (1600 train molecules): 1.15× instead of ≥ 10×.
* Training, steps/s, steps_per_execution=8, jit_compile=false (TrainConfig default) (1600 train molecules, |B| = 1): 1.20× instead of ≥ 1.5×.
* Inference, mol/s, precomputed descriptors (legacy: 1 molecule per call; new: batch 256) (1000 molecules): 7.51× instead of ≥ 10×.

### Analysis

**Measurement conditions.** Final reference measurement of the code of commit
`6090d43` (with the BLAS-thread limit of the descriptor workers and the new execution defaults). No
other heavy job ran: the 1-minute load average was 1.3 (new) and 3.0 (legacy) at the
start, and the measurement itself adds about 2-3 (parallel suites, TensorFlow
threads). The 15-minute average (5-6) still contains an earlier control run. The
repetitions spread by ≤ 12 % (`times_s`). A first full run ten minutes earlier gave the
same picture (training 2.36× instead of 2.28× with the preset settings, inference from
descriptors 8.2× instead of 7.5×; files not kept). Both runs used the working tree of
commit `6090d43` before it was committed, hence "uncommitted changes: True" with the
git SHA of its parent `2ff3f84`. The field `measured_tree` of both result files names
`6090d43` as the measured code state; it was recorded afterwards, without measuring
again. Future reference runs should be made from a committed state.

**Missed targets, stated plainly.** Six of the speed targets of the refactoring are
still missed: preprocessing of the aspirin-like molecule in one process (16.8× instead of
20×), bytes on disk for both molecules (0.45× / 0.47× instead of 3× smaller), the
input pipeline (1.15× instead of 10×), training with the `TrainConfig` default
`steps_per_execution = 8` without XLA (1.20× instead of 1.5×) and inference from
precomputed descriptors (7.5× instead of 10×). Met: preprocessing of the
stachyose-like molecule (26×), memory per molecule (8.8× / 10×) and training with the
settings of the thesis presets (`steps_per_execution = 8`, `jit_compile = true`:
2.28×).

**Preprocessing, 1 process (aspirin-like 16.8×, stachyose-like 26×).** The descriptor
kernel is vectorized per molecule (`compute_descriptors`, no Python loop over atom
pairs). For the 21-atom aspirin-like molecule a frame takes about 0.26 ms against
4.3 ms in the legacy `create_grid` + `create_matrices` + pandas path. At this size a
frame is about 20 NumPy calls on tiny arrays, so the fixed per-call overhead of NumPy
dominates; more speed would need vectorization *across* frames, which was not
attempted. For the 87-atom stachyose-like molecule the BLAS products of
`grid.cell_aggregates` dominate; there the target is met.

**Preprocessing and inference with several processes.** The descriptor
workers (`build_dataset`, `Potential.predict(n_workers > 1)`) now start with one
BLAS/OpenMP thread each (`OMP_NUM_THREADS`, `OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS`, … set only while
the workers are spawned; the parent process keeps its settings). Before, every worker
started an OpenBLAS pool with one thread per CPU and 10 workers oversubscribed the
machine. Control run, stachyose-like 200 frames, 10 workers, same machine:

| BLAS threads per worker | median of 3 builds | mol/s |
|---|---|---|
| default (before the limit) | 24.98 s | 8 |
| 1 (current code) | 0.44 s | 453 |
| (1 process, for comparison) | 0.71 s | 282 |

In the reference run the parallel build is now faster than the serial one
(stachyose-like 0.46 s vs 0.68 s, aspirin-like 0.44 s vs 0.51 s; before the limit: 26.4 s and
1.1 s). With these small workloads the start of 10 "spawn" processes takes most of the time (≈ 0.4 s, estimated from
the aspirin-like build: 0.44 s in parallel for 0.51 s of serial work), which is also why `Potential.predict` with 10 workers on 1000
small molecules (2 061 mol/s) is still slower than with one process (2 708 mol/s;
before the limit: 824 mol/s). Several workers pay off for large datasets, not for a few
thousand small frames.

**Bytes per molecule on disk (0.45× instead of ≥ 3× smaller).** The legacy pickles
are gzip-compressed, and gzip removes most of the zero padding of the legacy arrays.
The new format stores uncompressed `.npy` files on purpose, so that the splits can be
memory-mapped and read without unpacking. In RAM, which is the limiting resource in
the thesis setting (26.8 GB of legacy features for stachyose), the
new format is 8.8× (aspirin-like) and 10× (stachyose-like) smaller, so that target is
met. A compressed archive copy would fix the disk ratio but not the working-set size.

**Input pipeline (1.15× instead of 10×).** The target assumed that `iterrows`
dominates the legacy pipeline. It does not: the legacy rows already hold padded
float32 arrays, and one row costs about 0.14 ms, close to the per-element overhead of
`tf.data` itself. The new pipeline needs about 0.12 ms per molecule, also mostly
`tf.data` overhead (`numpy_function` read, F_i reconstruction). It is not the
bottleneck of training: at ≈ 8 300 mol/s it delivers more than 10× the molecules the
fastest training step consumes (720 steps/s).

**Training (default 1.20×, presets 2.28×).** With |B| = 1 a step is the forward and
backward pass of one 21-atom molecule (≈ 3 ms). The legacy step was already a
`tf.function`, so removing the host overhead (no `tf.constant` per step, no per-step
`.numpy()`) only brings the plain step to the legacy rate (0.99×). The
speed-ups come from the two execution options: `steps_per_execution
= 8` +20 % (+30 % with XLA), `jit_compile = true` +77 % / +91 %, together 2.28× the
legacy rate. Validation profits from batching (5.0×).

**Inference from precomputed descriptors (7.5× instead of 10×).** The new path runs
one model call per 256 molecules, 0.11 ms per molecule, against 0.84 ms per molecule
in the legacy loop (one `tf.function` call per molecule). The batched call is no
longer dominated by call overhead but by the forward pass itself; this was not
optimized further. From positions the end-to-end rate is 15.6× the legacy
`create_dataset` + `evaluate_model` path; the descriptors (≈ 4 100 mol/s) now dominate.

**Decision on the execution defaults.** Conditions: `steps_per_execution = 8`
bit-identical to 1, and XLA with K = 8 at least 1.5× the legacy rate with a passed
equivalence check. Both hold (max weight difference 0.0 after one epoch; 2.28×;
equivalence passed), so:

* `train.steps_per_execution = 8` is the `TrainConfig` default and is set in the four
  thesis presets. It is bit-identical to K = 1, also with dropout 0.2 and with XLA
  (tests `test_steps_per_execution_equivalent`, K ∈ {4, 5, 8}).
* `train.jit_compile = true` is set in the presets `paracetamol`, `aspirin`,
  `ac-ala3-nhme` and `stachyose` only. The `TrainConfig` default stays `false`, and
  `legacy-head.toml` and the test profiles are numerically unchanged.
* **XLA and dropout:** the presets use dropout 0.2, and under XLA dropout draws other
  random masks than without XLA. Runs are statistically equivalent but not bit-identical
  to non-XLA runs with the same seed; without dropout both agree to rounding (the XLA
  check above uses dropout 0). For bit-for-bit comparisons with a non-XLA run use
  `--set train.jit_compile=false`.
* If XLA is not available on a platform, the trainer logs a warning, trains without
  XLA and records `jit_compile = false` in the run's `config.json`.
* XLA compiles once per atom count, which costs nothing for the single-molecule
  datasets of the thesis.
<!-- END MANUAL ANALYSIS -->

## Method

* **Same runtime.** Both implementations run in the same virtual environment (`.venv`,
  same TensorFlow build and thread settings). The legacy code (`Neural-Network/` at
  commit `9413bfd`, unchanged) is exported with `git archive` into a temporary
  directory (`tests/golden/legacy.py`) and runs in its own process with
  `TF_USE_LEGACY_KERAS=1` (tf_keras); `lrmlp` runs in a separate process with Keras 3.
* **Workloads.** Deterministic synthetic molecules from `tests/golden/synthetic.py`
  (Lennard-Jones energies): 2000 aspirin-like frames (21 atoms, grid G-A: Δg = 1 Å,
  l_max = 6) and 200 stachyose-like frames (87 atoms, G-C: Δg = 2 Å, l_max = 4);
  `--quick` uses 200 / 20. Both processes generate the same arrays (checked by a
  SHA-256 over E, F, R, z).
* **Profile.** Grid assignment `legacy` and the network of `configs/legacy-head.toml`
  (embedding 64-128-128-128, K1 = 30 / 6, K2 = 4 / 2, fitting 128 + 2 residual blocks,
  dropout 0) for both implementations; N_max is taken from the data. Split 0.8 / 0.1 /
  0.1, shuffle buffer 1000.
* **Timing.** `time.perf_counter`, median of at least 3 repetitions (`--repeats`).
  Preprocessing: whole `create_dataset` / `build_dataset` call. Input pipeline: one
  pass over the training split without a model (after one warm-up pass; dataset
  construction reported separately as `load`). Training: one warm-up epoch, then 3
  windows of 2 epochs on the same model, energy loss only, one molecule per step
  (|B| = 1). Inference: 1000 molecules; legacy as in `evaluate.py` (one
  `tf.function` call per molecule on the preprocessed test pickle), new with
  `Potential.predict_descriptors` / `Potential.predict` and `batch_size = 256`.
* **Observation hooks.** The legacy code is not modified. For the training and
  inference loops the dataset returned by `create_tf_dataset` is wrapped by an
  iterator that records time stamps, and `Training.get_model` is replaced by a call of
  the unchanged `Model.get_model` after `clear_session()` and a fixed seed.

## Mixed precision

Mixed precision is not used and not benchmarked. The molecule energy
is the sum of the atomic energies and has a magnitude of |E| ≈ 4·10⁵ kcal/mol for
aspirin. float16 overflows at 65 504; bfloat16 has 8 significand bits, i.e. a
resolution of about 2·10³ kcal/mol at that magnitude, three orders of magnitude above
the target MAE of ≈ 1.7 kcal/mol. A loss-scaling optimizer does not help, because the
problem is the representable precision of the summed energy, not gradient underflow.

## Scope

Training with more than one molecule per optimizer step (|B| > 1) is not part of this
benchmark and not part of the code: the thesis trains with |B| = 1 (p. 51) and names
larger batches as future work (Chapter 7.4). The batched paths measured here
(validation, inference) do not change the result, only the number of model calls.

## Reproducing

```sh
source .venv/bin/activate
python benchmarks/run_benchmarks.py --impl new --suite all --out NEW.json
TF_USE_LEGACY_KERAS=1 PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    python benchmarks/run_benchmarks.py --impl legacy --suite all --out LEGACY.json
python benchmarks/compare.py LEGACY.json NEW.json --check-equivalence --markdown docs/benchmarks.md
```

Runtime of the runs on this page: legacy 140 s, new
125 s, plus the equivalence check. See
`benchmarks/README.md`.
